record.title: OpenAI introduces LifeVal, an evaluation of AI agents on everyday-life tasks
record.summary: OpenAI introduced LifeVal, an evaluation of AI performance on everyday-life tasks selected using American and multinational time-use datasets and supplemented by a demographically representative survey that the public page says included 3,995 respondents, while the linked paper’s methods section specifies n=3,837 for the willingness-to-pay survey; the difference is unresolved. Its public page reports selected task scores of 90.4%–100% on illustrated workflows, but does not identify which model produced the examples or provide an overall aggregate result or detailed open protocol. The design and scores are first-party; independent replication and real-world user outcomes are not established.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: OpenAI published LifeVal on 2 November 2026 as an evaluation intended to track model performance on everyday-life tasks involving personal-assistant workflows.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: OpenAI says its public LifeVal page used the American Time Use Survey and Multinational Time Use Study and supplemented them with a demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents; the linked paper separately specifies n=3,837 for its willingness-to-pay survey, and the discrepancy is unresolved.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: OpenAI reports selected LifeVal task scores between 90.4% and 100% across examples including kindergarten selection, flood-volunteer coordination, home search, remote game setup and diabetes-related meal planning; the inspected page does not identify which model produced these examples and does not present them as an overall aggregate score.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected public release does not establish which model generated the selected examples, independent replication, broad task-set representativeness, comparative performance across providers or real-world user outcomes.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The linked LifeVal paper specifies a willingness-to-pay survey sample of n=3,837 in §3.1, differing from the 3,995 respondents stated on the official webpage; the materials inspected do not explain the difference.

contradictory_evidence: OpenAI’s public LifeVal page (2 Nov, lines 57–59) reports a survey of 3,995 respondents, while the linked paper (3 Nov, §3.1, lines 112–124) specifies n=3,837 for the willingness-to-pay survey. Both are first-party descriptions; the reason for the difference is unresolved.

evidence_gaps.description: The inspected release does not expose the full task set, scoring protocol, task-level failure cases or implementation details needed for independent execution.
No independent evaluation or real-world user study was inspected to validate the reported task scores or whether they predict useful assistance.
The inspected public LifeVal page does not identify which model produced the selected task-example scores.

The official webpage reports 3,995 survey respondents, while linked paper §3.1 reports n=3,837 for the willingness-to-pay survey. The scope or reason for the difference is not specified in the inspected materials.

brief.importance_rationale: If the approach and reported scores generalize, evaluating agents on everyday tasks grounded in time-use data can change model and product choices beyond academic question-answering benchmarks; the public evidence remains first-party and methodologically incomplete.
limitations: All benchmark-design and performance claims are from OpenAI, the benchmark developer.
The public page shows selected task-level examples, not an aggregate benchmark result or a provider-matched comparison.
The evaluation page does not establish that the tasks, score construction or survey preferences generalize beyond the described population and workflows.
No independent reproduction or real-world user outcome evaluation was located in this bounded review.
The inspected LifeVal page does not identify which model produced the selected example scores.

OpenAI’s Nov 2 webpage reports 3,995 survey respondents; the linked Nov 3 paper §3.1 specifies n=3,837 for the willingness-to-pay survey. The reason and scope of this difference are not explained in the inspected sources.

Its public page reports selected task scores of 90.4%–100% on illustrated workflows, but does not identify which model produced the examples or provide an overall aggregate result or detailed open protocol. The design and scores are first-party; independent replication and real-world user outcomes are not established.

technical.claimed_result: OpenAI reports selected LifeVal task scores from 90.4% to 100% on illustrated workflows; the inspected page does not identify the evaluated model or report a single aggregate score.
technical.demonstrated_result: OpenAI published the LifeVal description and first-party examples on Nov 2, 2026.
technical.implementation_status: Public description only; full evaluation artifacts and scoring details were not inspected.
technical.mechanism: Task suite intended to measure practical personal-assistant workflows, informed by time-use data and a survey about user-valued tasks.
technical.regime: OpenAI-selected everyday workflows spanning caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finance, shopping and government services; model identity for the illustrated scores is not stated on the inspected page; The webpage reports 3,995 survey respondents; the linked paper specifies n=3,837 for the willingness-to-pay survey, and the difference is unresolved.
technical.reproducibility: The inspected official page does not provide a detailed scoring protocol or accessible benchmark task set; independent execution was not performed. The webpage and linked paper also give different survey counts (3,995 and 3,837 respectively); the inspected sources do not reconcile them.
technical.strongest_baseline: No provider-matched baseline was included in the inspected public release.

brief.title: OpenAI introduces LifeVal, an evaluation of AI agents on everyday-life tasks
brief.why_it_matters: Agent evaluation often emphasizes academic or narrow task benchmarks. LifeVal makes everyday assistance, including multi-step administrative and household workflows, an explicit evaluation target. Its value depends on how representative and reproducible the private task set and scoring method prove to be.
